name: Ethosuximide
drug_class: Succinimide anticonvulsant; T-type calcium channel blocker

discovery.note: Developed in the 1950s among succinimide compounds screened for activity against pentylenetetrazol-induced seizures.

tagline: Narrow-spectrum first choice for childhood absence epilepsy
summary: Ethosuximide is a succinimide anticonvulsant used specifically for absence seizures. A large 2010 trial confirmed it as the preferred first-line treatment for childhood absence epilepsy.
mechanism: Absence seizures arise from rhythmic 3 Hz spike-and-wave oscillations in thalamocortical circuits driven by low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons. Ethosuximide reduces these T-type currents, interrupting the oscillation.
It has little effect on tonic-clonic or focal seizures, so it is not used where these coexist without another agent.

history.title: Clinical studies
history.detail: Ethosuximide is evaluated as a less toxic alternative to trimethadione for absence seizures.

history.title: Mechanism
history.detail: Coulter and colleagues show that ethosuximide reduces low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons.

history.title: Childhood Absence Epilepsy trial
history.detail: Glauser et al. (NEJM) find ethosuximide and valproate more effective than lamotrigine, with ethosuximide better tolerated cognitively than valproate.

history.title: ILAE evidence review
history.detail: The International League Against Epilepsy rates ethosuximide and valproate as having the strongest evidence for initial monotherapy of childhood absence epilepsy.

pk.half_life: about 30 hours in children, 50–60 hours in adults
pk.excretion: renal, as metabolites and about 20% unchanged

facts: Ethosuximide is ineffective against generalised tonic-clonic seizures, which is why valproate is preferred when absences and tonic-clonic seizures coexist.

references.title: NEJM: Ethosuximide, Valproic Acid, and Lamotrigine in Childhood Absence Epilepsy (2010)
